Verification Workflow

screens.title: FBX Import Basics
screens.narratorSegment: FBX is the common transport format for models and baked animation. When you drag an FBX into Unity, the engine processes geometry, hierarchy, and any animation tracks embedded in the file. However, Unity’s default import settings are conservative and often not optimized for real-time character use. A frequent example is incorrect scale or transform inheritance from the exporter: models may import at an unexpected size or with rotated axes. Another common issue is that the default animation becomes a single long clip usually called Take 001, which may contain multiple distinct actions concatenated together. That is why you must open the Inspector and review the Model, Rig, Animation, and Materials tabs. Model lets you check Scale Factor and Read/Write settings, Rig determines whether Mecanim treats the skeleton as Humanoid or Generic, and Animation is where clip splitting happens. A misconception to avoid is trusting the automatic mapping for Humanoid rigs without visual verification. Even if the Avatar appears green, some bones may be misassigned. Always Configure Avatar and visually confirm bone mapping. Remember: import is not a one-click step — it’s a verification workflow that prevents noisy issues later in production.

screens.title: Inspector Tabs: Model, Rig, Animation
screens.narratorSegment: The Inspector is where import becomes deliberate. Start by selecting your FBX in the Project window and scanning the Model tab to confirm scale, mesh compression, and import materials. Next, move to the Rig tab. This is the decision point for animation type: set Humanoid for bipedal characters so you can retarget animations, or Generic for non-humanoid models and props. After choosing the type, click Apply. Then click Configure Avatar to visually map bones: red or yellow markers mean something needs correction. Once the rig is valid, open the Animation tab. Here you will see the animation timeline and the Clips section. Add new clips with the plus button and define precise start and end frames. Enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cycles that must repeat. A common misconception is to skip Configure Avatar when the preview shows motion; even a green avatar can hide incorrect bone orientation that causes subtle distortions. The reliable flow is Model → Rig → Apply → Configure Avatar → Animation → Split Clips → Apply. Following these steps every time reduces surprises in-scene and keeps your animation pipeline predictable.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Inspector Tabs
Step-by-step
Model
Check Scale Factor, import settings, and meshes. Fix orientation or scale before animating.
Rig
Choose Humanoid or Generic. Click Apply, then Configure Avatar to map bones.
Animation
Split clips, set frame ranges, enable Loop Time and Loop Pose when needed.
Misconception: Setting Humanoid automatically fixes all bone mapping. Reality: Configure Avatar is required to verify and correct mappings for reliable retargeting.
Concrete Scenario

You import a Mixamo character, set Rig to Humanoid, apply, then open Configure Avatar. You see a missing toe bone mapping marked yellow. You assign the correct bone and save. Without this, retargeting a different animation will distort the foot.

Key Takeaway

Run the same Inspector flow for every FBX to catch rig and clip problems early.

screens.title: Humanoid vs Generic Rigs
screens.narratorSegment: Humanoid and Generic are the two primary animation types in Unity’s Rig settings. Choose Humanoid when your model has a human-like skeleton. This choice activates Mecanim’s mapping and retargeting system so an animation made for one humanoid model can often be used on another, even with different proportions. Retargeting is powerful: you can reuse a walk created for one character on many characters without rebuilding animations. The key step after choosing Humanoid is Configure Avatar. Unity attempts automatic mapping, but you must visually verify shoulders, spine, hips, and limbs. Generic is for non-humanoid rigs like quadrupeds, vehicles, or props; animations are applied directly to the model’s bone hierarchy and are not retargetable by Mecanim. A common misconception is that Humanoid will always produce perfect results — it won’t if the T-pose deviates or if bone names are unconventional. If Configure Avatar highlights mismatches or a T-pose is different, correct the T-pose in your DCC exporter or adjust the avatar mapping. Choosing the correct type and verifying the avatar ensures animation fidelity and reusability across characters. Humanoid vs Generic Rigs means use humanoid for bipedal characters to enable retargeting; use generic when mecanim’s mapping is not appropriate.. In practical terms, when to choose humanoid and how it enables animation retargeting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Humanoid vs Generic
Humanoid
Retargeting enabled
  • Maps bones to a standard avatar definition.
  • Enables applying animations from other humanoid characters.
  • Requires correct T-pose and verified bone mapping.
Example: Reusing a walk cycle from one character across a cast without re-authoring the animation.
Generic
Direct bone hierarchy
  • Applies animation to the model’s existing bones directly.
  • Ideal for non-humanoid rigs, vehicles, or specialized skeletons.
  • No Mecanim retargeting; relies on authoring per model.
Misconception: Generic is weaker. Reality: It’s the correct choice for non-humanoid setups and preserves exact bone relationships.
Key Takeaway

Choose the rig type based on skeleton shape and reuse goals; always configure and verify the avatar after switching to Humanoid.

screens.title: Configure Avatar: Mapping Bones Correctly
screens.narratorSegment: Configure Avatar is the visual mapping step that connects your model’s bones to Unity’s Humanoid avatar definition. Open Configure Avatar after setting the Rig type to Humanoid and clicking Apply. Unity will show a skeletal overlay where each required slot should be assigned. Green means correct, yellow warns of possible issues, and red indicates a missing or clearly wrong mapping. Begin by confirming the root, hips, spine, neck, head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. If a bone is wrong, drag the correct bone from the hierarchy into the slot. Common errors involve extra joints or different naming conventions from different DCC exporters. A common misconception is that a green avatar guarantees perfect animation; green only means required mappings exist, not that axes or local rotations match expectations. After you finish, use the Pose preview to set the model to a T-pose if needed. If the T-pose is not recoverable in Unity, correct the bind pose in your source DCC and re-export. Verifying avatar mapping avoids stretched limbs and strange retargeted motions later in the pipeline. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Configure Avatar
Checklist
  • Confirm required slots are filled: Hips, Spine, Head, Arms, Legs.
  • Resolve yellow/red markers by assigning bones manually.
  • Use Pose preview to check T-pose orientation and local rotations.
Concrete example: If the left arm is flipped, the wrist bone may have an inverted local rotation. Correcting the bone assignment or fixing the exporter’s joint orientation resolves the issue.
Pro Tip

If the source T-pose differs from Unity’s, it's often faster to fix the pose in your DCC application and re-export rather than trying to compensate with avatar mapping alone.

Common Mistake

Ignoring yellow markers because the model ‘looks fine’ — small mapping errors become visible when retargeting different animations.

Key Takeaway

Configure Avatar is required for reliable humanoid retargeting — verify every required bone and the T-pose.

screens.title: Splitting Animation Clips
screens.narratorSegment: Many FBX exports include multiple actions concatenated into one long timeline. Splitting clips lets you create discrete Animation Clips such as Idle, Walk, and Run that the Animator Controller can use. In the Animation tab’s Clips section, click the plus to add a new clip, give it a clear name, and set precise start and end frames. Use the preview scrubber to find the exact frame where the action begins and ends. A helpful strategy is to mark an exact foot contact frame for walk cycles; this reduces visible sliding. Enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cycles. Loop Time repeats the clip, while Loop Pose attempts to blend the end and start poses to prevent a pop. A common error is choosing start/end frames that include a small pose transition from the previous action; this creates a hitch at boundaries. Always scrub frame-by-frame if necessary. After creating clips, click Apply to save the clip definitions. Preview each named clip in isolation to verify timing and smoothness before using them in an Animator Controller. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Splitting Clips
Step-by-step
  1. Open the Animation tab for the FBX asset.
  2. Click + under Clips to add a new clip and name it.
  3. Set Start and End frames precisely using the scrubber.
  4. Enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cycles; click Apply.
Example: Isolate Idle from frames 0–45, Walk from 46–120. Check foot contacts to align loops.
Example Card
You add two clips, name them Idle and Walk. Idle is looped and requires minimal pose change at the end. Walk must have matching start/end foot positions. Use Loop Pose to blend their boundary.
Common Mistake

Using approximate frames so the first and last frames differ; this creates a popping loop. Scrub precisely and preview at playback speed.

Key Takeaway

Precise frame selection and Loop Pose are essential for seamless cyclic animations.

screens.title: Loop Time & Loop Pose
screens.narratorSegment: Loop Time and Loop Pose are clip-level settings that make cycles like idle and walk repeat cleanly. Loop Time instructs Unity to play the clip repeatedly. If your clip’s first and last poses do not match exactly, you will see a pop when the clip restarts. Loop Pose attempts to smooth or reconcile that transition by adjusting pose data at the boundaries, reducing visible popping. Loop Pose does not fix badly authored animations; it helps when the start and end are close but not perfect. A concrete example: a walk cycle where the last frame shows the right foot slightly ahead of the first frame — enabling Loop Pose can reduce the small positional jump. A common misconception is that Loop Pose will correct dramatically different poses or inconsistent root motion; it will not. If the cycle is fundamentally mismatched, re-edit frame ranges or fix the source animation in your DCC tool. Always preview looped playback at actual game frame rates. If motion still jerks, refine frame boundaries or adjust the animation in the authoring package. Loop Time & Loop Pose means use loop time to repeat a clip and loop pose to smooth small start/end mismatches; redo the animation if mismatches are large.. In practical terms, making cycle animations repeat without visible jumps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use Loop Time to repeat a clip and Loop Pose to smooth small start/end mismatches; redo the animation if mismatches are large.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Loop Time & Loop Pose
Loop Time

Repeats the clip continuously. Use this for idles, walks, and any cyclic motions.

When to use
  • Idle, breathing, repeated gestures.
  • Walk cycles where footsteps repeat.
Loop Pose

Attempts to match start and end poses to avoid pops. Helpful for small mismatches but not a fix for badly authored cycles.

Misconception

Loop Pose will not repair completely different start and end poses. If the animation is misaligned, adjust frame ranges or fix in the source file.

Key Takeaway

Use Loop Time for repetition and Loop Pose to smooth minor mismatches. Always preview at runtime speed to validate.

screens.title: Root Motion Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Root Motion means the animation itself moves the model’s root bone, so the character’s transform is driven by the animation curves rather than by external scripts. When you enable Apply Root Motion on an Animator, Unity uses the root transform from the animation to update the GameObject’s position and rotation. This produces accurate stride length and body displacement that matches the visual motion, which can dramatically improve realism. Use root motion when animation displacement is authoritative for a character’s locomotion, and ensure your character controller complements rather than fights the animation. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Root Motion Explained
What it is

Root Motion uses the animation’s root bone curves to drive the GameObject transform, so the character moves exactly as the animation dictates.

Why use it
  • Accurate foot placement and natural translation.
  • Useful for cinematic or tightly synchronized movement.
When to avoid

If you need deterministic physics-driven movement, network smoothing, or simple controller-driven displacement, prefer script-driven motion and keep Apply Root Motion off.

Common Mistake

Allowing both root motion and a script to set position — this creates doubled movement and jitter.

Key Takeaway

Decide whether animation or script owns translation. Don’t let both move the character at once.

screens.title: Animation-driven vs Script-driven Movement
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between animation-driven and script-driven movement is a design and technical decision. Animation-driven movement, enabled by Apply Root Motion, gives natural displacement that matches the artist’s intent. It’s excellent for animations where precise foot placement, momentum, and non-linear motion matter. Script-driven movement usually means your controller sets the transform or applies forces. This is preferred when you need consistent physics interactions, predictable networked movement, or granular player input control. A common example: in a platformer with tight player input, script-driven movement ensures consistent jump distances and reliable collision responses. In contrast, a cinematic or a complex melee attack where the body shifts dramatically might be better as root motion to preserve artist-authored movement. Misconceptions often arise when people assume root motion conflicts with physics — it can work with physics if implemented carefully, but it requires coordination between the animator and the character controller. The practical rule: if animation displacement must be authoritative for gameplay fidelity, use root motion; otherwise, use script-driven movement and keep animations in-place. screens.title: Common Import Issues & Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring issues appear during animation import. First, the wrong Rig type: if you set Generic for a bipedal character, you lose Mecanim retargeting. Fix: switch to Humanoid, Apply, then Configure Avatar. Second, imprecise frame ranges when splitting clips cause extra frames or pops. Fix: refine start and end frames and preview at playback speed. Third, T-pose mismatch leads to distorted limbs when mapping to the Humanoid avatar. Fix: correct the T-pose in your source DCC or remap bones carefully in Configure Avatar. Fourth, scale or rotation mismatch comes from exporter unit settings or axis conventions. Fix: re-export with consistent units or adjust Scale Factor in the Model tab. Finally, root motion that doesn't move the character in-scene usually means Apply Root Motion is off on the Animator or a script is overriding transform updates. Fix by enabling Apply Root Motion if animation should drive movement, or remove root displacement if you prefer script control. Keep backups of FBX files and use version control to track changes when troubleshooting complex animation setups. Character walks in place in scene but moves in preview.

screens.title: Activity — Importing and Splitting a Character
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through importing a sample FBX and splitting its animations. First, download a multi-clip FBX such as a Mixamo character that contains Idle and Walk within one timeline. Drag the FBX into your Unity Project window. Select the asset and open the Rig tab. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to bring animated characters into Unity and prepare their animation data for gameplay. We start with the FBX import process and move through the Inspector tabs you must use: Model, Rig, Animation, and Materials. You will practice setting an animation type to Humanoid or Generic, applying avatar configuration to verify bone mapping, and splitting a long timeline into discrete clips such as Idle and Walk. We’ll also explain Loop Time and Loop Pose so cycles play smoothly, and unpack Root Motion — what it is, why it can improve realism, and how to avoid conflicting movement from scripts. Finally, you will see common mistakes to watch for, like wrong rig type, bad frame ranges, and mismatched T-poses. By the end, you'll be able to import an FBX, split clips precisely, enable loop settings, and decide whether to apply root motion in a gameplay situation. Think about a character that should walk precisely where its footsteps land; understanding these settings helps keep animation and motion synchronized.

These objectives guide the practical steps you will master. First, you will correctly import 3D models that contain animation data into Unity, ensuring the inspector settings are intentionally chosen rather than accepting defaults. Second, you will learn to configure animation clip settings in the Inspector — split long timelines into precise clips, name them meaningfully, and use Loop Time and Loop Pose so cycles are smooth. Third, you will be able to manage multiple animation clips from one FBX file, adjusting start and end frames carefully to avoid visual glitches. Fourth, you will understand the concept of Root Motion, how animation-driven displacement differs from script-driven movement, and when to enable Apply Root Motion in your Animator. Each objective includes a competence milestone so you can verify that the animation plays correctly in preview and in-scene. For example, after splitting Idle and Walk clips you will preview each and confirm that Loop Time produces a seamless cycle. These skills are essential for producing characters that animate and move reliably within gameplay.

This second objectives slide focuses on verification and troubleshooting. You will learn to inspect avatar mapping after switching to Humanoid and to correct any misidentified bones. You will test the preview window and watch root transform curves like Position(Y) and Rotation to detect unintended displacement. You will learn the signs of common problems: wrong rig type that prevents retargeting, imprecise frame ranges that add extra frames at clip boundaries, and mismatched T-poses that distort limb orientation. The verification workflow: import, set Rig, Apply, Configure Avatar, switch to Animation tab, split clips, enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cycles, then preview each clip in isolation. For root motion, preview the position curves; if displacement appears and you want animation-driven movement, enable Apply Root Motion on the Animator. This objective ensures you can not only perform the steps, but also recognize and fix the most frequent errors during import.

FBX is the common transport format for models and baked animation. When you drag an FBX into Unity, the engine processes geometry, hierarchy, and any animation tracks embedded in the file. However, Unity’s default import settings are conservative and often not optimized for real-time character use. A frequent example is incorrect scale or transform inheritance from the exporter: models may import at an unexpected size or with rotated axes. Another common issue is that the default animation becomes a single long clip usually called Take 001, which may contain multiple distinct actions concatenated together. That is why you must open the Inspector and review the Model, Rig, Animation, and Materials tabs. Model lets you check Scale Factor and Read/Write settings, Rig determines whether Mecanim treats the skeleton as Humanoid or Generic, and Animation is where clip splitting happens. A misconception to avoid is trusting the automatic mapping for Humanoid rigs without visual verification. Even if the Avatar appears green, some bones may be misassigned. Always Configure Avatar and visually confirm bone mapping. Remember: import is not a one-click step — it’s a verification workflow that prevents noisy issues later in production.

The Inspector is where import becomes deliberate. Start by selecting your FBX in the Project window and scanning the Model tab to confirm scale, mesh compression, and import materials. Next, move to the Rig tab. This is the decision point for animation type: set Humanoid for bipedal characters so you can retarget animations, or Generic for non-humanoid models and props. After choosing the type, click Apply. Then click Configure Avatar to visually map bones: red or yellow markers mean something needs correction. Once the rig is valid, open the Animation tab. Here you will see the animation timeline and the Clips section. Add new clips with the plus button and define precise start and end frames. Enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cycles that must repeat. A common misconception is to skip Configure Avatar when the preview shows motion; even a green avatar can hide incorrect bone orientation that causes subtle distortions. The reliable flow is Model → Rig → Apply → Configure Avatar → Animation → Split Clips → Apply. Following these steps every time reduces surprises in-scene and keeps your animation pipeline predictable.

Humanoid and Generic are the two primary animation types in Unity’s Rig settings. Choose Humanoid when your model has a human-like skeleton. This choice activates Mecanim’s mapping and retargeting system so an animation made for one humanoid model can often be used on another, even with different proportions. Retargeting is powerful: you can reuse a walk created for one character on many characters without rebuilding animations. The key step after choosing Humanoid is Configure Avatar. Unity attempts automatic mapping, but you must visually verify shoulders, spine, hips, and limbs. Generic is for non-humanoid rigs like quadrupeds, vehicles, or props; animations are applied directly to the model’s bone hierarchy and are not retargetable by Mecanim. A common misconception is that Humanoid will always produce perfect results — it won’t if the T-pose deviates or if bone names are unconventional. If Configure Avatar highlights mismatches or a T-pose is different, correct the T-pose in your DCC exporter or adjust the avatar mapping. Choosing the correct type and verifying the avatar ensures animation fidelity and reusability across characters. Humanoid vs Generic Rigs means use humanoid for bipedal characters to enable retargeting; use generic when mecanim’s mapping is not appropriate.. In practical terms, when to choose humanoid and how it enables animation retargeting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configure Avatar is the visual mapping step that connects your model’s bones to Unity’s Humanoid avatar definition. Open Configure Avatar after setting the Rig type to Humanoid and clicking Apply. Unity will show a skeletal overlay where each required slot should be assigned. Green means correct, yellow warns of possible issues, and red indicates a missing or clearly wrong mapping. Begin by confirming the root, hips, spine, neck, head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. If a bone is wrong, drag the correct bone from the hierarchy into the slot. Common errors involve extra joints or different naming conventions from different DCC exporters. A common misconception is that a green avatar guarantees perfect animation; green only means required mappings exist, not that axes or local rotations match expectations. After you finish, use the Pose preview to set the model to a T-pose if needed. If the T-pose is not recoverable in Unity, correct the bind pose in your source DCC and re-export. Verifying avatar mapping avoids stretched limbs and strange retargeted motions later in the pipeline. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In the Animation tab’s Clips section, click the plus to add a new clip, give it a clear name, and set precise start and end frames. Use the preview scrubber to find the exact frame where the action begins and ends. A helpful strategy is to mark an exact foot contact frame for walk cycles; this reduces visible sliding. Enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cycles. Loop Time repeats the clip, while Loop Pose attempts to blend the end and start poses to prevent a pop. A common error is choosing start/end frames that include a small pose transition from the previous action; this creates a hitch at boundaries. Always scrub frame-by-frame if necessary. After creating clips, click Apply to save the clip definitions. Preview each named clip in isolation to verify timing and smoothness before using them in an Animator Controller. Loop Time and Loop Pose are clip-level settings that make cycles like idle and walk repeat cleanly. Loop Time instructs Unity to play the clip repeatedly. If your clip’s first and last poses do not match exactly, you will see a pop when the clip restarts. Loop Pose attempts to smooth or reconcile that transition by adjusting pose data at the boundaries, reducing visible popping. Loop Pose does not fix badly authored animations; it helps when the start and end are close but not perfect. A concrete example: a walk cycle where the last frame shows the right foot slightly ahead of the first frame — enabling Loop Pose can reduce the small positional jump. A common misconception is that Loop Pose will correct dramatically different poses or inconsistent root motion; it will not. If the cycle is fundamentally mismatched, re-edit frame ranges or fix the source animation in your DCC tool. Always preview looped playback at actual game frame rates. Choosing between animation-driven and script-driven movement is a design and technical decision. Animation-driven movement, enabled by Apply Root Motion, gives natural displacement that matches the artist’s intent. It’s excellent for animations where precise foot placement, momentum, and non-linear motion matter. Script-driven movement usually means your controller sets the transform or applies forces. This is preferred when you need consistent physics interactions, predictable networked movement, or granular player input control. A common example: in a platformer with tight player input, script-driven movement ensures consistent jump distances and reliable collision responses. In contrast, a cinematic or a complex melee attack where the body shifts dramatically might be better as root motion to preserve artist-authored movement. Misconceptions often arise when people assume root motion conflicts with physics — it can work with physics if implemented carefully, but it requires coordination between the animator and the character controller. The practical rule: if animation displacement must be authoritative for gameplay fidelity, use root motion; otherwise, use script-driven movement and keep animations in-place. Several recurring issues appear during animation import. First, the wrong Rig type: if you set Generic for a bipedal character, you lose Mecanim retargeting. Fix: switch to Humanoid, Apply, then Configure Avatar. Second, imprecise frame ranges when splitting clips cause extra frames or pops. Fix: refine start and end frames and preview at playback speed. Third, T-pose mismatch leads to distorted limbs when mapping to the Humanoid avatar. Fix: correct the T-pose in your source DCC or remap bones carefully in Configure Avatar. Fourth, scale or rotation mismatch comes from exporter unit settings or axis conventions. Fix: re-export with consistent units or adjust Scale Factor in the Model tab. Finally, root motion that doesn't move the character in-scene usually means Apply Root Motion is off on the Animator or a script is overriding transform updates. Fix by enabling Apply Root Motion if animation should drive movement, or remove root displacement if you prefer script control. Keep backups of FBX files and use version control to track changes when troubleshooting complex animation setups. This hands-on activity walks you through importing a sample FBX and splitting its animations. First, download a multi-clip FBX such as a Mixamo character that contains Idle and Walk within one timeline. Drag the FBX into your Unity Project window. Select the asset and open the Rig tab. Set Animation Type to Humanoid and click Apply. Then click Configure Avatar and verify all required bone slots; resolve any red or yellow markers by dragging bones into place. Next, open the Animation tab. Under Clips, click + twice to create Idle and Walk clips. Name them and use the scrubber to find precise start and end frames for each. Enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for both. Click Apply to save. Finally, preview each clip in the Inspector to ensure smooth looping and inspect the Root Transform Position curves if you expect displacement. If the Walk clip shows vertical or forward curves, decide whether to enable Apply Root Motion at runtime. These are the concise concepts to remember. FBX is the transport format that carries meshes, skeletons, and baked animation. Humanoid Rig maps your skeleton to Unity’s standard avatar and enables retargeting across similarly structured characters. Generic Rig keeps animation tied to the original bone hierarchy, best for non-humanoid assets. Animation Clips are named segments extracted from a longer timeline; define precise start and end frames to avoid visual glitches. Loop Time repeats a clip; Loop Pose smooths minor mismatches between start and end poses. Keep these concepts in mind when importing and preparing animations so you make consistent, predictable choices that match your project’s technical and design needs. Remember these practical rules: always run the Model→Rig→Configure Avatar→Animation sequence when importing, enable Loop Time and Loop Pose for cyclic clips, and preview root transform curves to detect displacement. If you will let animation move the character, enable Apply Root Motion and avoid moving the transform in code. If you need deterministic physics or predictable network sync, keep root motion off and drive movement by script. When you split clips from a single FBX timeline, pick start and end frames precisely to avoid pops. Finally, keep backups of original FBX assets and use version control so you can revert exports if mapping or pose corrections require re-exports.
